volumes.title: Setting Out from the Bridge
volumes.text:
My name is Perpetua Dunn, land surveyor, and this atlas is the record of one season's work. In May the council of Emberwick engaged me to map the Lowlands, from the south end of the town bridge to the sea wall, in twelve sheets. No proper map of that country existed. There was only a sketch in the Guildhall on which the largest feature was a gravy stain.

I set out on the twelfth with my apprentice, Tam, who is fourteen and can already draw a straighter line than I can; a pony named Bracket; a plane table; a brass chain; and forty red flags.

The first sheet shows very little: the bridge, the Lowland road, and four miles of pasture. But every map must start from one fixed point. Ours is a cross I cut in the last stone of the parapet.

volumes.title: The Baseline at Larkacre
volumes.text:
A map of the Lowlands is built from triangles, and the triangles are built from one line measured on the ground with all the care a surveyor has. I am Perpetua Dunn, and in the second week of my survey I measured that line across Larkacre pasture, five miles south of Emberwick.

It runs one mile exactly: eighty lengths of the brass chain, laid end to end, each checked twice. My apprentice Tam held the forward end. I held the rear and kept the book. We began at dawn, before the heat could stretch the brass, and finished at four.

We lost an hour to a brown cow, which ate the red flag marking the far end and had to be followed until we were sure where it had been. Tam has drawn her on Sheet Two, very small, in the corner. I have let her stay.

volumes.title: The Village of Three Names
volumes.text:
Sheet Three of this atlas covers the country around a village eight miles south of Emberwick, and I, Perpetua Dunn, surveyor, regret that I cannot tell you for certain what the village is called. I asked.

The miller said it was Nether Sedge and always had been. The woman at the inn said Sedgeby, and that the miller came from elsewhere. The children simply call it the Village, and looked at me kindly, as at someone who had not known the name of the sun.

A map must say something. My apprentice Tam suggested we write both names, the larger for the one most people used. So we sat by the pump for a morning and counted. Sedgeby won by eleven voices, Nether Sedge is in smaller letters beneath, and the pump is marked, at the children's request, with a dot.

volumes.title: The Windmill Triangle
volumes.text:
In flat country a surveyor needs tall things to sight on, and the Lowlands south of Emberwick offer only windmills. On Sheet Four I, Perpetua Dunn, fixed the whole middle district from three of them: Sedge Mill, Cobb's Mill and the white mill at Farthing Green.

The method is simple. From each mill you measure the angles to the other two, and since you already know one distance, the rest follows by arithmetic. My apprentice Tam climbed to each cap with the instrument on his back. I stayed below and held the pony.

The angles of a triangle should add to a hundred and eighty degrees. Ours came to a hundred and eighty and a hair. I spent two days hunting the hair, and found it. Cobb's Mill is a post mill, and the miller had turned the whole building to face the wind between our visits.

volumes.title: Drains and Dykes
volumes.text:
The Lowlands would be a lake if left alone. What keeps them pasture is ditches, hundreds of miles of them, and on Sheet Five of this atlas I, Perpetua Dunn, had to draw every one within a ten-mile square south of Emberwick.

I could not have done it without Corwen, the dyke-reeve, who is eighty and has cleaned those drains since boyhood. He walked ahead of us with a long hooked pole, naming them as he went: Long Lode, Crooked Lode, Widow's Drain, and the Sulk, which runs backwards in a west wind. My apprentice Tam wrote the names. I measured.

Corwen had never seen a map. When I showed him the finished sheet, with its blue lines, he studied it a long while. Then he put one finger on a ditch I had drawn straight, and said it had a kink in it. He was right.

volumes.title: The Field with No Owner
volumes.text:
Every old sketch of the Lowlands leaves one place blank, about twelve miles south of Emberwick, and marks it only with the word "doubtful". I am Perpetua Dunn, surveyor, and in July I went with my apprentice Tam to remove the doubt. It is Sheet Six of this atlas.

We found a broad level field of forty acres, with good grass and no hedge, no gate and no cattle. The farms on every side stop short of it. Nobody claims it.

The reason came from a woman cutting rushes at its edge. In summer, she said, it is a field. From November to March it is a lake, two feet deep, with swans. No one wants to own a thing that is only there half the year. I have drawn it in both colours, green hatched with blue, and written in its local name: Sometimes.

volumes.title: Sounding Hollow Mere
volumes.text:
Hollow Mere is the one large water in the Lowlands, a mile and a quarter long, fifteen miles south of Emberwick. To put it on Sheet Seven I, Perpetua Dunn, needed its shape and its depth, and so for four days my survey went by boat.

The shape was easy: we walked the shore with the chain. The depth was patient work. A fisherman called Ham rowed us back and forth while my apprentice Tam let down a lead weight on a knotted cord and called out the knots. I wrote down two hundred and six soundings.

The mere is shallow, with one deep place near the middle, nineteen feet, where the water comes up cold. Ham says a great bell lies there. We sounded the spot four times and brought up only weed, but I have marked it with a small bell just the same.

volumes.title: The Great Flat
volumes.text:
Sheet Eight of this atlas is nearly empty, and I wish to say that this is accurate. I am Perpetua Dunn, surveyor. In August my apprentice Tam and I crossed the Great Flat, the middle of the Lowlands, twenty miles south of Emberwick, where for a whole day's walk there is no house, no mill and no rise of ground higher than a molehill.

A surveyor needs things to measure between. Here there was grass, and one thorn tree, bent by the wind into the shape of a person running. We measured to the thorn from four directions simply for the comfort of it.

Tam was troubled by so much white paper. In the end he drew the thorn tree, and then, along the top margin, a small careful row of the clouds as they stood that afternoon. It is against all practice. I signed the sheet anyway.

volumes.title: Tower in the Fog
volumes.text:
In September the weather broke over the Lowlands, and Sheet Nine of this atlas was made mostly indoors. I am Perpetua Dunn, surveyor; my apprentice Tam and I were then twenty-five miles south of Emberwick, at the hamlet of Withy End.

We needed one last sight, to the old watch tower on Rook Knoll, the only landmark in the southern district. For six days it stood in fog. We lodged with a basket-maker, and while we waited I inked the summer's pencil work at her kitchen table and Tam lettered names, his tongue between his teeth.

On the seventh morning the fog lifted for perhaps ten minutes. Tam ran out with the instrument in his socks. He had the angle read and written down before the tower faded again, and came in soaked to the knee and extremely pleased. The basket-maker gave him the largest egg.

volumes.title: The Sea Wall
volumes.text:
The Lowlands end at a bank of clay twelve feet high, and beyond it is the sea. I am Perpetua Dunn, surveyor, and on the second of October, thirty-one miles and nearly five months from Emberwick bridge, my apprentice Tam and I led the pony up onto the sea wall and looked over.

Behind us lay everything we had measured: green, ruled with ditches, dotted with mills. In front was grey water to the edge of the sky. Bracket, who had never seen the sea, stood with her ears forward and would not be led down for half an hour.

We chained along the top of the wall for two days, with the tide coming and going at our elbow. Past the last inked line, Sheet Ten is left bare, which is as near as I can come to drawing the sea.

volumes.title: Closing the Traverse
volumes.text:
A survey is proved by coming home. I am Perpetua Dunn, and through the summer my apprentice Tam and I had carried our measurements south across the Lowlands from a cross cut on Emberwick bridge. In October we carried them north again by a different road, mapping as we went. That is Sheet Eleven.

The test is this. If every angle and every chain length has been true, the figures will lead you back to your starting mark and say that you are standing on it. If not, they will say you are standing somewhere else, and by how much.

We reached the bridge on the twentieth, at dusk. I worked the sums twice by lantern on the parapet. After seventy miles of measuring, the figures placed the cross four feet from where it is. Tam asked if that was good. I told him it would do.

volumes.title: The Atlas Bound
volumes.text:
The Atlas of the Lowlands was finished at Emberwick in the last week of November. I, Perpetua Dunn, surveyor, inked the twelfth sheet myself. It is the index: the whole country from the bridge to the sea wall on one page, with the other eleven sheets shown as numbered squares.

The council had the sheets bound in green cloth and placed in the town library, where anyone may consult them. On the first day the dyke-reeve, Corwen, came in his best coat to see that the kink was still in his ditch. It was.

Tam's name is on the title page beside mine. He has earned it, and the brown cow and the clouds besides. The pony has gone to grass at Larkacre, in sight of our baseline. As for me, I notice that the council's sketch of the Northern Fells is mostly stain.

volumes.title: The Mouth at Greywater
volumes.text:
This is the survey of the river Ember from the sea to its source, made by me, Ottoline Pike, in one spring. I began where the river ends, on the Grey Coast, at the harbour of Greywater, on the first of April.

A river's mouth is the hardest part to draw, because it will not stay still. At high water the Ember here is half a mile wide. Six hours later it is a brown thread between two mudbanks, and the fishing boats sit on their sides like tired dogs.

I have hired a flat-bottomed boat, the Moorhen, and a boatman named Gil Tansy, who speaks about once an hour and is always right. We spent three days sounding the bar with a pole. I marked the channel at low water and at high, in two inks, and set my first peg on the harbour wall. Mile nought.

volumes.title: Where the Salt Ends
volumes.text:
Four miles above its mouth at Greywater, the river Ember stops being sea. I am Ottoline Pike, surveying the river from the coast to its source, and I wished to mark on my chart the exact place where the tide gives up.

Gil Tansy, my boatman, said the eel-catchers know it as the Heron Stakes, a row of old posts across a bend. To be sure, we moored the Moorhen there for a full day. Every hour I tasted the water, which is not in any manual, and tied a ribbon to a stake at the level it had reached.

The flood tide crept up to the stakes, lifted the boat eleven inches, paused, and went back. Below that bend the water was brackish at noon. Above it, sweet all day. I have drawn a line across the river there and written "tide ends," with the date.

volumes.title: The Marsh Reaches
volumes.text:
Between the tide's end and the town of Emberwick the river Ember crosses the marsh, and takes nineteen miles to cover what a crow would do in eight. I am Ottoline Pike, river surveyor, and those nineteen miles cost me twelve days.

The river here is not one stream but several, plaited together among the reeds. Channels part, wander, and join again. Some end in a pool full of lilies. My boatman, Gil Tansy, poled the Moorhen up each in turn while I took bearings, and more than once we rounded a bend to find our own marker ribbon waiting for us.

I have drawn the main channel in a firm line and the others in fine ones. A bittern boomed the whole time, somewhere to the left. We never saw it. It is on the chart all the same, as a small question mark with a beak.

volumes.title: Under Emberwick Bridge
volumes.text:
Twenty-three miles from the sea the river Ember passes under the three stone arches of Emberwick bridge. I am Ottoline Pike, surveying the river from mouth to source, and here I stopped a week to measure not where the water goes but how much of it there is.

The method needs a known width, a known depth and a known speed. Width and depth I took from the bridge with a weighted line, arch by arch. For speed, my boatman Gil Tansy dropped painted corks from the upstream parapet while I stood below with a watch and timed them through.

A crowd gathered. Small boys began betting on the corks. By my reckoning the Ember carries past Emberwick, on an ordinary April day, enough water to fill the market square knee-deep every minute. The mayor asked me not to put it that way.

volumes.title: The Pennybrook Joins
volumes.text:
A mile above Emberwick bridge a small stream enters the river Ember from the east. This is the Pennybrook. I am Ottoline Pike, river surveyor, and since a river is the sum of what flows into it, I left the main stream for three days to follow this one.

It is only four miles long, and a child could jump it nearly anywhere. Yet the people of Emberwick and Marrowby speak of it with great respect, and showed me a meadow it runs through, with a pear tree, geese, and a footbridge that has a step in the middle. The brook, they say, has moved twice and may again.

My boatman, Gil Tansy, studied the banks and gave it as his opinion that it will. I have therefore drawn the Pennybrook in pencil, not ink. It is the only pencil line on the whole chart.

volumes.title: The Weir at Tulley's Mill
volumes.text:
Thirty miles from the sea the river Ember meets its first wall. I am Ottoline Pike, surveying the river upstream toward its source, and at Tulley's Mill a stone weir crosses the whole stream, four feet high, with the water sliding over it like bent glass.

The mill has ground Emberwick's flour for more than two hundred years. The miller let me measure the fall, the mill race and the great wheel, which is sixteen feet across and turns nine times a minute when the sluice is open. In return I was to tell him how deep his pond was. He had always wondered.

A boat cannot climb a weir. My boatman, Gil Tansy, and the miller's two sons carried the Moorhen round on their shoulders, upside down, like a long green beetle. The pond is eleven feet deep by the sluice. The miller had guessed forty.

volumes.title: The Long Pool
volumes.text:
Above Tulley's Mill the river Ember slows and deepens into a reach the anglers call the Long Pool: three miles of dark, quiet water under alders, thirty-three miles from the sea. I am Ottoline Pike, river surveyor, and I took its soundings in the first week of May.

My boatman, Gil Tansy, let the Moorhen drift while I lowered the lead. The bottom is clean gravel, twelve to fifteen feet down, and so clear that I could see the weight land. Swallows drank beside us. It was the easiest work of the whole survey, and I did not hurry it.

On the second day a very large pike rose under the lead line, looked at it, and sank away again. Gil spoke unprompted for the first time in a week. He said, "Relation of yours." I have marked the place on the chart with my initial.

volumes.title: Into the Gorge
volumes.text:
Forty miles from the sea the river Ember comes out of the Northern Fells through a gorge, and there a boat can go no farther. I am Ottoline Pike, surveying the river to its source. On the twelfth of May we drew the Moorhen up on the shingle and turned her over, and my boatman, Gil Tansy, became my chainman.

The gorge is a mile long and sixty feet deep, cut in grey rock, with ferns on every ledge. The river, so slow lower down, is here loud and white and in a hurry. I measured its fall: ninety feet in the mile.

At the top the valley opens, and the drove road crosses on an old bridge of flat stone slabs. We ate our bread sitting on it. From here the survey goes on foot, and the river, I suspect, will keep getting younger.

volumes.title: Black Beck and White Beck
volumes.text:
Four miles above the gorge, high in the Northern Fells, the river Ember divides in two, and a surveyor must decide which branch keeps the name. I am Ottoline Pike, and I had come forty-five miles from the sea to find a fork with no signpost.

The shepherds call the left stream Black Beck, for its peaty water, and the right one White Beck, for its stones. I asked them which was the Ember. They shrugged. It had never mattered to the sheep.

The rule is to follow the greater flow. My chainman, Gil Tansy, and I built a little dam of turf on each and measured how fast a bucket filled. Black Beck filled it in nine seconds. White Beck took fourteen. So the Ember is the dark one, and we turned left. White Beck is on the chart too, fairly drawn, as a tributary.

volumes.title: Spindle Force
volumes.text:
Forty-eight miles from the sea, the stream I have followed as the river Ember falls over a cliff. I am Ottoline Pike, river surveyor, and the waterfall is called Spindle Force: a single thin white thread dropping into a black pool, with a rowan tree leaning over the lip.

A fall must be measured, and there is only one honest way. My chainman, Gil Tansy, held my ankles. I lay on the wet rock at the top and let down the sounding line, the same lead that found the bottom of the harbour at Greywater, until I felt it touch the pool. Seventy-one feet.

We climbed round by a sheep track. Above the fall the land is open moor, the stream is a stride wide, and the wind smells of nothing but grass. Gil remarked that there could not be much river left. He sounded sorry.

volumes.title: Lantern Tarn
volumes.text:
Fifty miles from the sea, the stream I have surveyed as the river Ember runs out of a small round lake. I am Ottoline Pike. The shepherds call the lake Lantern Tarn, because on still evenings it holds the last light after the hills have gone dark.

I had half hoped it was the source. A tarn makes a tidy beginning, and my boots had worn through. We walked its shore with the chain, six hundred yards around, and my chainman, Gil Tansy, waded in with the pole to take its depth.

But at the far end, among rushes, a trickle no wider than my hand was running in. Water that runs in has come from somewhere. I closed the book and said we would find it in the morning. We slept in a shepherd's hut, and the tarn kept its light until nearly ten.

volumes.title: The Spring
volumes.text:
The river Ember begins under a grey rock the size of a kitchen table, on a hill called High Wick, fifty-one miles from the sea. I am Ottoline Pike, river surveyor, and I reached it on the twenty-sixth of May with my chainman, Gil Tansy, after eight weeks of following the water uphill.

The spring comes out of a crack in the rock into a basin of moss no larger than a hat. It is very cold. It fills, spills over one edge, and sets off downhill towards the tarn, the fall, the gorge, the mill, the bridge, the marsh and the sea, as if it knew the way.

I drove in my last peg and wrote the mileage on it. Then we each drank a cupful. Gil said it tasted the same as at Greywater, only without the salt, and that was the survey finished.

volumes.title: Where the Salt Way Began
volumes.text:
I am Wilmot Cray, and for forty years I mended the roads of this district with a shovel and a barrow. Now that I am retired I mean to walk a road that needs no mending, because it is not there.

The Salt Way once ran from the salt pans at Brinepan Cove on the Grey Coast to the market at Emberwick, forty miles inland. My grandmother, Nell Cray, drove a string of nine ponies along it as a girl. I have her waybook: twelve stages, each with a note in pencil, such as "mind the ford" and "good pie".

I started this morning from the cove. The pans are only square hollows in the turf now, with sea lavender growing in them. But a stone slipway still runs up from the beach, grooved by sledges, and points inland like a finger. I followed it.

volumes.title: The Hollow Way
volumes.text:
The second stage of the old Salt Way, from the Grey Coast towards Emberwick, climbs out of Brinepan Cove through gorse, and I, Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, found it by falling into it.

A road that carries loaded ponies for two hundred years wears down. Hooves loosen the soil, rain carries it off, and little by little the track sinks until it is a trench with banks above a walker's head. This one is nine feet deep and roofed over with hazel. From the field beside it you would see only a line of bushes.

Inside, it is green and still, like a room. The floor is worn rock with a groove down the middle. My grandmother's waybook says of this stage, "ponies know it." I walked a mile and a half without seeing the sky, and came out on the hilltop among larks.

volumes.title: A Milestone in a Garden
volumes.text:
Seven miles in from the Grey Coast, the old Salt Way to Emberwick disappears into the village of Furzeham. I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, walking the lost road by my grandmother's waybook, and for the third stage her note says only, "count the stones."

There were once milestones. I found one at last in a cottage garden, standing among the beans with a pan of water on top for the birds. The lettering was worn but could be read with a thumb: Emberwick, thirty-three miles.

The owner, Mrs Applin, said her grandfather had rolled it home in a barrow when the road was given up, thinking it too good to waste. She had not known what the numbers meant. I told her. She said she would look at the sparrows' bath with more respect, and gave me a bag of plums for the journey.

volumes.title: The Causeway under the Reeds
volumes.text:
The fourth stage of the old Salt Way crosses a corner of the marsh, eleven miles from the Grey Coast, and my grandmother's waybook says of it, "keep to the stakes." I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender. There are no stakes. There are reeds, taller than my hat.

But a road-mender knows that stone does not go away. I cut a long ash pole and went forward a step at a time, probing. To either side the pole sank in black mud to my hand. In front, a foot under the water, it struck something flat and hard.

That was the causeway: slabs laid by the salt carriers, drowned now, but as firm as the day they were set. I walked two miles on a road I could not see, with wet boots and great satisfaction. A heron watched the whole performance and plainly thought me unreliable.

volumes.title: The Packsaddle Inn
volumes.text:
Sixteen miles from the Grey Coast, on the fifth stage of the old Salt Way, my grandmother's waybook has its longest entry: "The Packsaddle. Good pie. Stable dry. Landlady sharp." I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, walking the lost road to Emberwick, and I had looked forward to this one.

There is no inn. There is a farmhouse, long and low, standing end-on to a field as if expecting somebody. But the farmer's wife, Mrs Dace, showed me the kitchen beams, which have nine iron hooks in a row for nine sets of harness, and a stable with stalls too small for any horse.

She had always wondered about the hooks. I read her my grandmother's note. She laughed at "sharp," said the pie at least could be managed, and it was: mutton and onion, eaten at the same hearth, some ninety years late.

volumes.title: The Ford Nobody Uses
volumes.text:
Twenty miles from the Grey Coast, halfway along the old Salt Way to Emberwick, a stream called the Withy Water crosses the line of the road. I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, and my grandmother's waybook says of this sixth stage, "mind the ford. Left of the alder."

A ford is the one part of a road that cannot be ploughed up. The alder was gone, but its stump was there, as broad as a cartwheel. I took off my boots and waded in to the left of it. Elsewhere the bed was soft silt. On the line it was cobbles, set tight, each the size of a loaf.

Minnows were holding station above the stones, exactly as if waiting to cross. I stood in the middle a while. Nine ponies had gone through here twice a week, and the stream had kept the place for them.

volumes.title: The Line of Old Thorns
volumes.text:
On its seventh stage the old Salt Way enters the Lowlands, twenty-four miles from the Grey Coast, and there the plough has had it. I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, walking the lost road to Emberwick, and I stood at a gate looking at eighty acres of barley and no track.

My grandmother's waybook says, "straight on by the thorns." It took me some time to see them: seven old hawthorns in a line across the field, each standing alone in the crop. They were once a roadside hedge. The farmer ploughs round them, without knowing why his grandfather did.

Then the wind moved the barley, and I saw the rest. Between the thorns ran a long stripe where the corn stood shorter and paler, on the stony ground of the old roadbed. I kept to the headland and walked beside my road to the far gate.

volumes.title: The Toll House in the Field
volumes.text:
Twenty-eight miles from the Grey Coast, in the middle of a Lowland pasture, stands an eight-sided house with a window on every side. I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, walking the vanished Salt Way to Emberwick, and I knew what it was at once. No one builds a house that shape unless they need to watch a road both ways.

The road is gone from its door and sheep graze to the step, but the old man who lives there, Mr Garrity, keeps the toll board on his kitchen wall: a pony laden, one farthing; a pony unladen, nothing; a pig, by agreement.

My grandmother's waybook says of this stage, "pay the man, he counts." I offered Mr Garrity a farthing for the look of the thing. He took it very gravely, wrote me a ticket, and opened his garden gate as wide as it would go.

volumes.title: The Crossroads with One Arm
volumes.text:
At thirty-one miles from the Grey Coast, deep in the Lowlands, the old Salt Way met three other roads, and my grandmother's waybook marks the spot with a cross and the words, "do not take the wrong one." I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, on the ninth stage of my walk to Emberwick.

The finger-post is still there, oak, silver with age. It has sockets for four arms and only one remaining, which points down a farm track and says "Sedgeby." The other three ways are ditch, hedge and turnip field.

I sat under it and worked the matter out as a road-mender would. The salt went north-east; and in that direction, across the turnips, I could make out a gap in the far hedge just the width of a laden pony. I thanked my grandmother, and took the right one.

volumes.title: The Green Lane
volumes.text:
For three miles of its tenth stage the old Salt Way is not lost at all. I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, thirty-four miles from the Grey Coast on my walk to Emberwick, and after days of reeds, barley and turnips I stepped through a hedge onto a broad lane of grass, with oaks along it.

Nobody has stoned or scraped it in ninety years, and it is in better order than some roads I was paid to keep. The turf is close and springy. The ruts are still there, softened, a pony's width apart.

My grandmother's waybook says of this stretch, "sing here, it's easy." I met a girl bringing five goats home, who told me it was just called the Lane and went nowhere. I said it went to the sea. She thought that over, and said she would try it on Saturday.

volumes.title: Why the Road Died
volumes.text:
Thirty-seven miles from the Grey Coast, the old Salt Way climbs a low rise, and from the top I, Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, could see the reason it was abandoned. The reason is another road.

It lies a mile to the east: the Lowland high road, raised and stoned, with a carrier's cart crawling along it. That road was made in my grandmother's girlhood. A pony carries two hundredweight on a track a yard wide. A cart carries a ton, but needs a real road under it. Once the carts could reach the coast, the pony strings were finished within ten years.

My grandmother's waybook says of this eleventh stage, "nearly there." Ahead, where the two roads draw together, I could see a clock tower and a line of lime trees. I mended that road for forty years, and found I could not be angry with either road.

volumes.title: The Last Stage
volumes.text:
The old Salt Way ends where Emberwick began, at the ford. I am Wilmot Cray, retired road-mender, and on the ninth day of my walk I came down a grassy bank to the river Ember, forty miles from the salt pans, a little below the stone bridge.

My grandmother's waybook says of the twelfth stage, "ford, bell, market, home." The gravel showed pale under the water. I could have used the bridge, a hundred yards off. I took my boots off instead, waded over to the knee, and touched the old ferry bell on the far bank, as she must have done.

The market clock said I was seven minutes early. I have given the waybook to the town library, with my own notes pencilled beside hers. The road is still not there. But it can be followed now, by anyone who cares to borrow the book.

volumes.title: Leaving Greywater
volumes.text:
I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and this book is my account of charting the Cinder Isles, which lie off the Grey Coast between ten and thirty miles out. The Harbour Board at Greywater engaged me in June, after a coal brig spent a night aground on an island that her chart said was a mile away.

The only chart in existence is ninety years old and drawn by nobody knows whom. It shows twelve islands. The fishermen of Greywater say there are eleven, and have said so, with some heat, for as long as anyone can remember.

I am to settle it. I have the cutter Sandpiper, a sextant, a lead line marked in fathoms, and Bess Tarrant, who has skippered these waters for thirty years and regards charts as a thing for people who do not know where they are. We sailed on the morning ebb.

volumes.title: Hearth Island
volumes.text:
The first and largest of the Cinder Isles is Hearth, ten miles off the Grey Coast, and I, Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, began my survey there because it has a harbour, a well and a bakery. It is two miles long and shaped something like a boot.

Charting an island means going round it slowly. Bess Tarrant, my skipper, kept the cutter Sandpiper close offshore while I took angles to the headlands and the ship's boy, Dab, swung the lead and sang out the depths.

The old chart had Hearth half a mile too far north and the harbour on the wrong side. The islanders, forty households, had never noticed, having no need of a chart to find their own front doors. The baker asked to see his shop on the new one. I drew it in, a very small square, and he gave me a loaf.

volumes.title: The Two Bellows
volumes.text:
North of Hearth in the Cinder Isles lie Great Bellows and Little Bellows, and the old chart draws them as one island. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, sent from Greywater to put these waters right, and I can report that the old chart was half correct.

At high water they are two: grassy humps a quarter of a mile apart. At low water a bar of shingle rises and joins them, and sheep walk across as if on business. For six hours they are one island, and then for six they are not.

My skipper, Bess Tarrant, asked how I meant to draw that. I timed the bar through four tides, sitting on Little Bellows with a watch and a flask of tea. It is on the chart as a dotted neck, with the words "dries three hours either side of low water." The sheep already knew.

volumes.title: Cinder Rock
volumes.text:
The fourth of the Cinder Isles gives the group its name and is the least welcoming. Cinder Rock is a black stack sixty feet high, with no beach, no grass and no place to put a foot. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and I charted it without touching it.

It belongs to the seabirds. Every ledge was packed with guillemots standing shoulder to shoulder like a crowd at a fair, and the noise reached us half a mile off. So did the smell.

My skipper, Bess Tarrant, sailed the Sandpiper round it twice at a respectful distance while I took its height by sextant and its position by angles to Hearth and the Bellows. The lead found forty fathoms close in: the rock goes down as steeply as it goes up. I have marked it "steep-to, birds," and that is all a sailor needs to know.

volumes.title: Kettle Island
volumes.text:
Kettle, the fifth of the Cinder Isles, is a ring of low rock around a lagoon, with one gap on the eastern side like a spout. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and after the bare black stack of Cinder Rock it was a pleasure to anchor in still water.

The gap is forty yards wide and two fathoms deep at half tide. My skipper, Bess Tarrant, took the Sandpiper through under jib alone, with the boy Dab calling depths from the bow. Inside, the lagoon is as round as a plate and so clear that I charted much of the bottom by looking over the side.

One person lives on Kettle: a retired sailmaker named Orrin, who keeps bees in nine straw hives. He told me heather honey is the only cargo the island ships. We left with a jar, and his hives are on the chart.

volumes.title: The Tongs
volumes.text:
North Tong and South Tong, the sixth and seventh of the Cinder Isles, lie side by side eighteen miles off the Grey Coast: two long thin ridges with a strait between them no wider than a village street. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and that strait needed sounding.

The trouble is the tide. It pours through the gap at six knots, first one way and then the other. My skipper, Bess Tarrant, would not take the cutter Sandpiper near it except at slack water, which lasts about twenty minutes.

So we waited at anchor, went through with the lead going as fast as the boy Dab could swing it, and came out the far end as the stream turned. We did that six times in three days. I have nine soundings from the strait, and I am prouder of them than of any hundred taken elsewhere.

volumes.title: Fog on Poker Reef
volumes.text:
Not everything in the Cinder Isles is an island. Between the Tongs and the outer group lies Poker Reef, a mile of rock that shows only as a line of broken water, and I, Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, was taking its bearings when the fog came down.

It arrived in ten minutes and took away the Tongs, the horizon and our own bowsprit. My skipper, Bess Tarrant, anchored at once in eight fathoms and set the boy Dab to ring the bell every minute. There was nothing else to be done. A chart-maker in fog is merely a passenger.

We lay there nineteen hours. I passed them inking soundings below, by lamp. Bess sat on deck, listening to the reef, and said afterwards she could tell where it was by the sound. When it cleared, the surf was breaking exactly where she had pointed. I marked it there.

volumes.title: The Keeper of Scuttle
volumes.text:
Scuttle, the eighth of the Cinder Isles, is a round green island with a lighthouse on it, twenty-two miles off the Grey Coast. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and I landed there for fresh water and came away with the most useful thing in my survey.

The keeper, Mrs Agnes Flint, has tended the light for twenty-six years. Every day she has written down the time and height of high water: nineteen ledgers, in a hand like copperplate. Nobody had asked her to, and nobody had ever come to read them.

A chart without tides is half a chart. With her figures I can say when the Bellows bar dries, when the Tongs run slack, and how deep the Kettle spout is at any hour. I copied for two days. She fed us on scones, and would accept in return only a promise of the finished chart.

volumes.title: The Grate
volumes.text:
The ninth of the Cinder Isles is hardly higher than the sea. The Grate is a low bank of sand and marram grass, twenty-five miles off the Grey Coast, with parallel sandbars lying off its southern shore like the bars of a fireplace. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and it gave me more trouble than any rock.

Rock stays where it is put. Sand does not. Mrs Flint of Scuttle light had warned me that the bars shift with every winter gale, and when I compared my soundings with the old chart, nothing agreed.

Two hundred seals were hauled out on the outermost bar. They watched the cutter Sandpiper go up and down with the lead. My skipper, Bess Tarrant, said they were laughing. I have drawn the bars as I found them and written across them, "these move," which is the truest thing on the sheet.

volumes.title: Ash Holm and Spark
volumes.text:
The two outermost of the Cinder Isles lie thirty miles off the Grey Coast, at the edge of the old chart. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and I reached them in the last week of August, the tenth and eleventh islands of my survey.

Ash Holm is a whaleback of rock and turf, where the fishermen of Hearth leave sheep for the summer. Spark, a mile beyond, is the smallest island I have ever charted: forty paces by twenty-five, with a spring, one stunted rowan and a cairn. I walked round it in two minutes and measured it with the boy Dab's fishing line.

That made eleven. I said so to my skipper, Bess Tarrant, who had told me as much in June. But the old chart shows a twelfth, three miles north-east of Spark, labelled, in faded ink, "the Ember." We set a course for it.

volumes.title: The Twelfth Island
volumes.text:
Three miles north-east of Spark, where a ninety-year-old chart of the Cinder Isles shows a twelfth island called the Ember, there is open sea. I am Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, and I looked at it from the deck of the cutter Sandpiper. My skipper, Bess Tarrant, was kind enough to say nothing.

But a chart-maker sounds before he believes. The lead had been finding twenty fathoms. It came up at four, then two, then one. There was a shoal under us, a hill of sand almost at the surface. Mrs Flint's ledgers at Scuttle light gave the lowest tide of the year for the next dawn, and we anchored.

At ten past five the sea drew back and a bank of wet sand rose out of it, pink in the early light. I rowed over and stood on it. It stayed for fifty minutes, and then it went out.

volumes.title: The Fair Chart
volumes.text:
I, Jonas Merrow, chart-maker, drew the fair copy of my chart of the Cinder Isles at Greywater in October, on one sheet of linen-backed paper. It shows eleven islands in firm black line, from Hearth to Spark.

It also shows a twelfth. The Ember is drawn in dots, with the note, "sand, dries for one hour at the lowest tides of the year." The old chart-maker was right, and so were the fishermen; it depends upon the day. Bess Tarrant, my skipper, looked at it a long time and allowed that a chart might have its uses.

One copy hangs in the harbour office. One went to Mrs Flint at Scuttle light, as promised, and one to the library at Emberwick. The baker's shop on Hearth is there, a very small square, and so are nine beehives on Kettle. A chart should show what matters.
